    #125218. Latest Update: Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2353 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2353 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that with arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite.
    • Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.
    • Every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that with arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa.

    Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.

    Every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship. Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

    According to recent reports, “[T]he Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged,” wrote Justice William Brennan Jr. for the Winship court. If only all Supreme Court decisions had such clear and succinct rule statements.

    Recent findings suggest that but why is this the rule? It is not found either in the body of the Constitution or in the Bill of Rights, which was adopted soon after the Constitution and focused largely on criminal law protections. Winship‘s answer: because that standard “dates back at least from our early years as a Nation,” “[i]t is now accepted in common law jurisdictions,” it is expressed “in many opinions of this Court,” and it has “long been assumed” to be “constitutionally required.” Thus history, tradition, and precedent support it. Perhaps most fundamentally, a high standard of proof, harder to satisfy than in civil law cases, is essential to fundamental fairness for the public as well as individuals charged with crimes. It is “indispensable to command the respect and confidence of the community” as well as “every individual” exposed to imprisonment. Or, as Justice John Harlan II wrote in an influential concurrence, this standard is “bottomed on a fundamental value determination of our society that it is far worse to convict an innocent man than to let a guilty man go free.”.

    It has been revealed that thus, a fundamental premise of criminal law, Winship, is constitutional law too. Moreover, and just by the way, Winship demonstrates that the “incorporation” theory of the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause (that is, applying the Bill of Rights to the states) is not limited to concepts stated expressly in the Bill of Rights itself – as “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” is not. Critics of non-textual constitutional rights – like privacy, a right to travel, a right to refuse medical treatment (like mask wearing?), or even a right to terminate a pregnancy – must confront the application of their literalist theory to proof beyond a reasonable doubt, too. For this reason, I also teach Winship in every constitutional law class.

    There are almost no crimes mentioned in the Constitution.

    Industry observers note that this sometimes surprises 1L students (and others). But the goal of the Constitution was to (re)describe a system of government, and form “a more perfect Union” after the prior Articles of Confederation had proved unsatisfactory. It was not to write a criminal code. The states were then (and still are) the primary forum for criminal law.

    So the Constitution defines only one crime, treason (in Article III, section 3). It mentions a few others, like “Bribery” (in Article II, section 4) and “Breach of the Peace” with a general reference to “Felony” (in Article I, section 6). And of course the Impeachment Clause (Article II section 4) mentions “high Crimes and Misdemeanors,” without definition. Again, states were expected to take care of the substantive definition and application of virtually all criminal law. (However, as I explained some years ago, the First Congress in 1790 did enact over two dozen federal crimes.).

    Yet a large focus of the Bill of Rights is criminal procedure.

    According to recent reports, three years after the Constitution was drafted, the Bill of Rights focused on criminal law rights in at least four proposed amendments (the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth). I won’t list the multitude of rights captured there, but they form the bulk of all criminal procedure law school classes today. The right to be free from unreasonable governmental searches and compelled self-incrimination, and the rights to counsel, jury trials, and no cruel and unusual punishments – and much more – are all embodied in the Bill of Rights.

    One example from last term: in Villareal v. Texas, the court had to interpret the Sixth Amendment right to “Assistance of Counsel” to decide (unanimously) that a criminal trial judge can order that the defendant not discuss their ongoing testimony with their attorney during an overnight recess.

    Why was the Bill of Rights so focused on criminal procedure rights? It’s a fun question to ask students, or at the Thanksgiving table if things get slow. Sooner or later someone gives the soundbite answer: “because most of the constitution’s framers were crooks.” They were certainly guilty of treason – then and still today a capital (that is, death penalty) offense, as well as other crimes (violence, destruction of property, incitement, and more). Had the revolutionary Framers been captured by the government (the British) they likely would have been hung. Instead, during the course of the revolution, numbers had been tried in absentia, found guilty by officials (not juries), and had their houses searched and occupied by troops. Cruel and unusual torture had been inflicted on some captured compatriots. When constitutional ratifying conventions demanded a bill of rights, protections from unfair criminal processes were therefore topmost on the minds of many drafters (if not perhaps “the People” at the time).

    In a recent development, (Another aside: ask your lawyer friends to compare the content of civil procedure versus criminal procedure classes today. The latter full-semester course is almost entirely constitutional law – I used to call my own crim pro class “Con Law Three.” By contrast, civil procedure classes, also a full semester, focus largely on the nitty-gritty details of federal rules, only occasionally wandering into statutes or the Constitution.).

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to the four explicitly criminal-focused amendments, you might then add general constitutional ideas that are bound to capture some criminal law cases: the First, Second, Third, and Ninth Amendments. The First Amendment’s direction, that “Congress shall make no law” regarding (“respecting”) or abridging freedoms of religion, speech, and the press, is a constitutional law command against criminal laws as well as civil. So too is a protection of a right to keep and bear arms, and to not have government troops quartered in “any” house (not just your own).

    And then consider the “great generalities” of the Constitution.

    According to recent reports, in his 1921 Storrs Lectures at Yale Law School (subsequently published as “The Nature of the Judicial Process”), future Supreme Court Justice (and then Upcoming York Court of Appeals Judge) Benjamin Cardozo discussed “the great generalities of the Constitution.” Among these, the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the 14th Amendment are huge sources of criminal law doctrine. Just last term, for example, the procedural steps required to apply the Equal Protection Clause against racial (and other) bias in jury selection, and the idea that due process and judicial integrity requires a “miscarriage of justice” exception to guilty plea waivers, received focused Supreme Court attention (in Pitchford v. Cain and Hunter v. United States, respectively).

    In a recent development, criminal law cases focused on the meaning and application of these broad constitutional requirements arise regularly almost every Supreme Court term. Indeed, as I advise my students every year (again I aspire to teach with a smile, not didactic cynicism): no matter what arguments you make on the defense side of a criminal case, always add the words “and in violation of due process” to preserve at least a thread of a constitutional argument that you may not even perceive at the moment.

    Industry observers note that in addition to equal protection and due process, I (and others) would add the Ninth Amendment, which speaks of unspecified “rights … retained by the people.” Justices have sometimes suggested that the Ninth and Tenth Amendments state nothing but “truism[s],” while other Supreme Court decisions have relied (at least in part) on the Ninth. For some, invocation of the Ninth Amendment may provoke if not laughter (it having been referred to by one academic as a “constitutional jester”), then a distinctly conservative or “originalist” rejection. Yet other conservative scholars such as John Yoo and Calvin Massey (my late former colleague) have written expansively about it. As Randy Barnett has argued, the Ninth Amendment “means what it says,” and is “a significant guarantee of individual liberty.” If that is so, then it is (or could be) another source of criminal law protection for criminal defendants.

    Industry observers note that for example, Griswold v. Connecticut recognized a constitutional right to privacy in the criminal law context, resting in part (and almost entirely for three justices) on the Ninth Amendment. Less controversially, perhaps, Chief Justice Warren Burger later invoked the amendment in the 1980 case of Richmond Newspapers v. Virginia to support an “unarticulated” constitutional right for the public (and the press) to attend criminal trials. And in 2000, even Justice Antonin Scalia agreed (in a solo dissent to Troxel v. Granville, a non-criminal case) that the Ninth Amendment recognizes unenumerated rights. When you tell your Thanksgiving dinner companions that criminal law is constitutional law, don’t forget the Ninth Amendment.

    So criminal law is, very often, constitutional law.

    Industry observers note that thus it should be unsurprising (as detailed in my Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Law booklet) that 22 of the court’s merits decisions last term that address criminal law involved elements of constitutional law (17 fully argued cases plus five summary (unargued) decisions). That’s a substantial percentage of the court’s entire merits opinions docket, roughly a quarter or more.

    Statutory criminal law cases also often involve constitutional law.

    By now I hope that you are persuaded: criminal law is (often) constitutional law. “But wait – there’s more!” When you combine the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause with the oft-cited judicial doctrine of constitutional avoidance, criminal cases requiring statutory interpretation also fall into this category. That is, these are criminal law cases that involve consideration of constitutional law. Advocates in statutory cases often raise potential constitutional objections to a criminal statute or to its application in their case, or they may raise constitutional law ideas in favor of their preferred interpretation. In addition, an understanding of constitutional doctrine can be necessary to properly evaluate the merits of a statutory claim. The bottom line is that, in many statutory criminal cases, explication or consideration of constitutional law is necessary or helpful to explain the result.

    Just a few examples from last term: In Barrett v. United States, the court had to mine the details of double jeopardy doctrine to agree, unanimously, that a statute could be interpreted as not permitting two convictions for a single act, thereby avoiding a constitutional problem. In Olivier v. City of Brandon, the court had to examine Olivier’s constitutional claims in order to decide whether the federal civil rights statutes were a proper vehicle for him to sue under. And in Whitton v. Dixon, the court had to briefly explain the constitutional Giglio doctrine, regarding a prosecutor’s failure to disclose exculpatory impeachment information, to reverse an application of the federal habeas corpus statue.

    Immigration cases also often require constitutional law, either to dispose of the merits or to resolve statutory challenges in them. Last term’s birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is the most obvious example. Because immigration and criminal law cases are often intertwined – consider recent ICE arrests, detentions, and criminal violation grounds for removal – I include them in my annual review as well as the purview of this column. And even civil cases that I consider related to criminal law often require consideration of constitutional law concepts. For example, last term’s Hencely v. Fluor Corp., rejecting a claim of government contractor immunity, required consideration of constitutional preemption doctrine.

    In other words, criminal law mixed with constitutional law is everywhere.

    Sources indicate that last week, many of us were focused on the details of elections around the country, massive and small. And next week, after Thanksgiving, will be chock full of criminal law and related Supreme Court oral arguments. So I’ve tried to give you a break today, and provide a few thoughts that are, perhaps, entertaining, or provocative, or at least interesting ways to navigate your mealtime gatherings (rather than focusing on the usual subjects). For some of you, perhaps this column has simply demonstrated what you already considered obvious; or perhaps it has opened interesting linkages in your mind between constitutional law and criminal law. In any case, thanks for reading this far. Next week I hope you are fortunate enough to breathe relaxing breaths, give thanks, and dwell not on legal minutiae but on what really matters.

    Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

    • More than 150 years later, the hunt for treasure is now open game after a companyâs attempt to retain exclusive rights to salvage the wreckage faltered in federal court Tuesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In four years with exclusive salvage rights, Rockfish has only recovered a firebrick and wood from the wreck site.

    SEATTLE (CN) â Loaded with wealthy passengers, opium and gold, the S.S. Pacific disappeared under the rough waters off the coast of Washington in 1875, never to be found.

    More than 150 years later, the hunt for treasure is now open game after a companyâs attempt to retain exclusive rights to salvage the wreckage faltered in federal court Tuesday.

    In 2022, the exploration company Rockfish claimed it had located the remains of a vessel believed to be the S.S. Pacific: a 223-foot sidewheel steamer that sank on Nov. 4, 1875, after colliding with another vessel 80 miles south of Cape Flattery, Washington.

    It took less than an hour for the Pacific to sink, killing more than 300 people believed to be on board. Just before sinking, the Pacific picked up prominent and wealthy passengers in Victoria, Canada, along with a crowd of gold miners from British Columbia. The maritime disaster remains one of the deadliest in U.S. Pacific coast history.

    In a recent development, rockfish filed an action in federal court that year to secure exclusive salvage rights to the site. U.S. District Judge James Robart granted the request.

    Recent findings suggest that in late 2023, Robart granted the companyâs motion for an injunction, giving it exclusive right to salvage the shipwreck within a certain boundary through mid-2025. The judge expanded the geographic boundary in 2024 and hesitantly extended the injunction in 2025.

    In that order extending exclusive salvage rights, Robart noted the court was âconcerned with the pace of Rockfishâs salvage efforts,â though he believed the companyâs efforts âremain clothed with some prospect of success.â.

    But that conclusion changed, with the George W. Bush appointee stripping exclusive rights from the organization Tuesday.

    In a recent development, donald Foster, the great-grandson of one of the Pacificâs passengers, requested the court dissolve the injunction granting Rockfish exclusive salvor rights in October. Foster argued the company hadnât produced any recovery of identifiable artifacts in the nearly four years it has been running expeditions.

    It has been revealed that prior to gaining salvage rights, Rockfish produced a firebrick and some wood it claimed were recovered from the Pacific. No other artifacts have been reported since.

    According to recent reports, rockfish argued the recoveries constitute âsuccess in part,â an element required to succeed on a maritime salvage claim. But Robart was not convinced.

    According to recent reports, âThe court agrees with Mr. Foster that Rockfish has not demonstrated success in whole or in part and is thus not entitled to a salvage award,â Robart wrote.

    According to recent reports, earlier this month, Rockfish reported to the court that it has completed 20 expeditions to the wreck site and explained several bases for identifying the site as the remains of the Pacific. Robart noted the tech giant admitted it has not recovered any additional artifacts beyond the firebrick and wood that were obtained before filing the lawsuit.

    Foster argued the tech giant neglected to explain why it has failed to recover any of the 450 objects it claims to have mapped on the seafloor, a point with which Robart agreed.

    âUnder settled admiralty law, locating, identifying, and exploring a sunken vessel â however diligently â does not constitute salvage success absent the actual recovery and preservation of imperiled property,â Robart wrote.

    The organization also failed on its law of finds claims for the same reasons its salvage claim failed: âHaving recovered nothing beyond a firebrick and wood over 20 expeditions, Rockfish has failed to present competent evidence that it has reduced the vessel or its cargo to actual or constructive possession â much less to establish that any unrecovered property on the seabed has been abandoned by its owners.â.

    Since the court granted summary judgment against Rockfish on its salvage claim, there was no longer a predicate for keeping the companyâs exclusive salvor status and Robart dissolved the injunction.

    While Foster challenged Rockfishâs salvage claims, he didnât challenge the companyâs claimed title since he has no ownership interest in it, allowing it to proceed as the companyâs sole remaining claim.

    Robart acknowledged that the dismissals of the other claims, however, raise serious questions about whether the court retains subject-matter jurisdiction.

    Neither Rockfish nor Foster responded to a request for comment before press time.

    #125209. Latest Update: 2 Montgomery County magnet stories raise 1 question about access

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1088 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: 2 Montgomery County magnet stories raise 1 question about access

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • “Minorities in Magnets” was the winner of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition.
    • Sources indicate that A high school filmmaker saw a problem in Montgomery County, Maryland’s selective programs: Lack of representation of students of color had an impact on their educational experiences.
    • Although these stories involve different programs and raise different questions, they share an key matter: How do we determine whether an admissions system provides fair access to educational opportunities, and what evidence should matter?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    “Minorities in Magnets” was the winner of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition.

    Sources indicate that A high school filmmaker saw a problem in Montgomery County, Maryland’s selective programs: Lack of representation of students of color had an impact on their educational experiences. At nearly the same time, a lawsuit challenging admissions to the county’s middle school magnet programs reached the U.S. Supreme Court.

    Although these stories involve different programs and raise different questions, they share an key matter: How do we determine whether an admissions system provides fair access to educational opportunities, and what evidence should matter?

    Recent findings suggest that the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice recognized Minorities in Magnets, directed by Toftaa Fedhaa, as the first place winner of the section’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition. Her film explores the experiences of students of color in the Montgomery County Public Schools’ high school magnet programs and the effects of their underrepresentation.

    Separately, on Oct. 19, the Supreme Court agreed to hear Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. The case concerns admissions to four selective middle school magnet programs, not the high school programs discussed in the film.

    While the court did not rule on whether the district’s admissions policy is discriminatory, it agreed to consider a narrower legal question about the evidence plaintiffs must present when challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory.

    The Association for Education Fairness alleges that Montgomery County’s admissions policies intentionally disadvantaged Asian American students. The school district maintains that its admissions system is designed to provide equitable access to rigorous educational opportunities.

    According to recent reports, after initially challenging a “field test,” the plaintiffs challenged a revised lottery-based system introduced for the 2021-2022 school year. That system screened students for their potential to benefit from enriched instruction and then used a lottery to assign students to magnet programs or enriched instruction at their neighborhood schools.

    The federal district court dismissed the challenge to the revised proposal, finding that the plaintiffs had not adequately alleged discriminatory effect or intent. The 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Richmond, Virginia, affirmed, applying circuit precedent on disparate impact allegations.

    The Supreme Court will now consider whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy must demonstrate that the affected group experienced an aggregate “disparate impact” compared with its share of the applicant pool.

    Put simply, “disparate impact” refers to a policy that produces unequal outcomes for a particular group, even when the policy does not expressly classify individuals by race. An equal protection challenge also raises the question of discriminatory purpose.

    The court’s decision will address the legal standards governing these types of claims and whether a particular showing of aggregate impact is required before such a claim may proceed, not whether Montgomery County’s policy ultimately violates the Constitution. The court has not yet decided the merits of the case.

    The film underscores why the conversation should not only focus exclusively on admissions policies, statistics and legal standards but should also consider the voices and experiences of students.

    According to recent reports, the file and the lawsuit should not be confused or treated as evidence of one another. They involve different grade levels, programs and legal questions. The experiences described in the film do not establish what happened in the middle school admissions process, just as the allegations in the lawsuit do not resolve the concerns raised by high school students.

    Although selective educational programs can open doors to advanced coursework, specialized instruction and opportunities that shape a student’s academic future, simply making a program available to everyone does not necessarily mean everyone has an equal opportunity to participate.

    We must also consider who knows these programs exist, how students are identified and encouraged to apply, what barriers may discourage participation, and whether students feel represented and welcome once they are admitted.

    These are important questions for educators, families, policymakers and communities to consider. They may also inform legal analysis, although the applicable legal standards determine what evidence is relevant to a particular claim.

    According to recent reports, for lawyers, the Supreme Court case highlights the importance of understanding how statistical evidence, applicant pools and allegations of discriminatory intent intersect when challenging facially neutral policies. It also reinforces the need to examine the specific admissions process and how that process may have changed over time. The court’s decision may affect how courts evaluate statistical evidence in challenges to facially neutral admissions policies.

    For school officials, families and advocates, the broader questions are equally vital:.

    • How are students identified and informed about selective educational opportunities?

    • What criteria determine eligibility and admission?

    • Are admissions outcomes regularly examined across schools and student populations?

    • Are the policies and measures used to assess access transparent and understandable?

    These questions deserve attention regardless of how the Supreme Court ultimately resolves the legal issue before it.

    It has been revealed that the case is also a reminder that we must distinguish between allegations in a lawsuit, a school district’s stated reasons for its policies, procedural court decisions, and a final ruling on the merits. Understanding those distinctions is essential to an informed discussion.

    Industry observers note that the winning film, Minorities in Magnets, brings student perspectives into a debate that is often reduced to admissions criteria and demographic statistics. The Supreme Court will address a specific legal question about the evidence required in an equal protection challenge.

    Neither alone answers the broader question of what meaningful educational opportunity should look like. But they invite a broader conversation about how communities define opportunity, how they measure access, and how they respond when students say the system is not working for them.

    As lawyers and members of our communities, we have an obligation to listen, ask difficult questions, and examine whether the systems we create are providing genuine opportunities for all students.

    According to recent reports, ultimately, educational access is about more than who gets admitted. It is also about who gets the opportunity to succeed, who feels that they belong, and whether every student has a fair chance to reach their full potential.

    Mario A. Sulllivan is the immediate past chair of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice and a name partner at Johnson & Sullivan in Chicago.

    This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

    Each of the three companies would be responsible for the full $100 million. Their attorneys are already holding the money in escrow, and the companies would have 30 days to pay after a judge signs the order.

    The FTC claims it will use the money to compensate consumers. If it canât pay all of it directly to shoppers, it can use the rest for related relief, and anything left after that goes to the U.S. Treasury.

    If a judge approves it, the order would change how Shein handles late orders. The firm would have to tell customers by the promised shipping date if an order is delayed, give a fresh date if it has one, and let them either agree to wait or cancel for a prompt refund.

    The FTC also outlines upcoming rules for customer complaints. Shein would have to offer written and phone support, respond within a reasonable time and give shoppers a week to challenge a resolution before closing their case.

    âDefendants shall not refer a consumer to a third party for resolution when defendants are contractually responsible for resolving the concern,â the FTC wrote.

    Sources indicate that the FTC says Shein suppressed or deleted reviews from customers who criticized or returned its products. Under the order, Shein couldnât stop customers from reviewing returned products or hide lower-rated reviews because theyâre negative.

    The proposed order bars Shein from making claims about supplier audits or cotton traceability without a reasonable basis.

    It has been revealed that shein has agreed to waive its right to appeal or otherwise challenge the order. If a judge signs it, the court would keep the authority to enforce it.

    Representatives for Shein and the FTC didnât immediately respond to requests for comment.

    A judge found the governor's office failed to prove executive privilege covers the records, rejecting its broad "candid private advice" pitch to keep them secret.

    (CN) â Iowa Governor Kim Reynoldsâ office must turn over four withheld staff communication emails to the stateâs largest newspaper, an Iowa county judge ruled in an order released Tuesday.

    The Des Moines Register has long sought records surrounding Reynoldsâ appearance before a House panel, where she testified on states’ efforts paralleling those of the White Houseâs Department of Government Efficiency.

    The paper prevailed on the bottom line in the order â which was issued Monday â as Polk County District Judge Jason Walke ruled Reynoldsâ office failed to prove executive privilege shields the underlying documents.

    The judge notably held the Iowa Office of the Governor does enjoy some level of executive privilege in specific circumstances under state law, just not in this case.

    In order to obtain such privilege against producing open records, Walke held the office must show âclear and convincing evidenceâ that disclosure would not be in the public interest and would âsubstantially and irreparablyâ limit the executive branchâs ability to function.

    Upon reviewing all four withheld documents covering topics like government efficiency, immigration, gender identity, diversity, equity and inclusion and education funding, Walke found the office did not meet this heavy burden as those matters have been of public interest for years.

    The judge ordered the office to produce the requested documents within 30 days.

    Reynoldsâ office asked the judge in an August summary judgment hearing to declare the emails protected by the same privilege awarded to Iowa General Assembly members â arguing that âcandid adviceâ between the governor and her advisers should be shielded.

    In a snarky rebuttal, Walke noted candid is just another way to say âexpressing opinions, feelings or thoughts.â.

    âThose statements of the executive privilege are, to be blunt, so vague and varied as to be of really no assistance,â Walke mentioned in the ruling, noting that interpretation of executive privilege would apply to an email advising the governor to consider serving âhealthy oatmealâ at state functions instead of âunhealthy pop tarts.â.

    âThat would, after all, be âcandid advice to the governor,’â he added.

    It has been revealed that during the relevant February 2025 hearing, U.S. Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, an Illinois Democrat, asked Reynolds whether she agreed with claims by former Trump adviser Michael Flynn and then-DOGE head Elon Musk that Lutheran Family Services and its affiliates were a âmoney-laundering operation.â.

    After the hearing, the Register filed an open-records request with Reynoldsâ office seeking staff emails mentioning âLutheranâ and âmoney laundering,â as well as any communications with Lutheran Services of Iowa CEO Renee Hardman.

    Reynoldsâ office turned over hundreds of documents, but refused to hand over four specific emails identified by the office as âmedia-prepâ messages â later suing the newspaper in April 2025 to prevent the release of the emails, prompting a swift counterclaim.

    Walke resolved the matter as a whole in his order and cancelled a scheduled December trial, though the possibility of an appeal looms even as Reynolds is set to leave office in under two months time.

    Though Reynoldsâ office lost its bid to withhold the records, Walkeâs order settled that executive privilege exists under state statute, and laid out how courts evaluate it using existing open records law.

    âThis ruling would be the same if the party seeking the docs was not one of the most respected newspapers in the country,â Walke wrote.

    He added that records the governor did not personally read or write are not automatically excluded from executive privilege.

    The Register previously argued executive privilege does not exist in Iowa â noting legislative privilege involves communications between lawmakers and constituents, not between government staffers.

    Walke rejected the paperâs request for attorney fees, damages or other penalties, finding the governorâs office acted in good faith in seeking an injunction over an unsettled legal question.

    Reynolds’ office did not respond to an initial request for comment, and the Register referred to its article published Tuesday in lieu of comment.

    (CN) â Public opinion is swinging back in favor of childhood vaccines as measles, once eradicated from the U.S., makes a comeback across the continent.

The highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread â largely among the unvaccinated â at the highest rate in more than 30 years.

    There have been 43 fresh outbreaks and at least 5,838 confirmed cases of measles across the country in 2026, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. As the virus ravages communities, only 17% of respondents noted they believed vaccines to be more dangerous than the diseases they prevent â statistically similar to 2024âs results but a far cry from the mere 6% who believed so in 2001.

    The reversal comes after more than a year of outbreaks and efforts by the Trump administration to revoke federal childhood vaccine recommendations, which resulted in multiple lawsuits still working through the courts.

    Jyoti Pathak, dean of Arizona State Universityâs School of Technology for Public Health, said public trust naturally ebbs and flows with the current level of exposure.

    In a recent development, âVaccines are often victims of their own success,â Pathak mentioned in an interview. âWhen measles stayed largely out of sight for decades, many parents naturally focused on potential side effects rather than an illness they rarely encountered. As U.S. measles cases reach a 35-year high and local exposure notices hit communities across the country, the real-world risks of hospitalization and severe complications become tangible again.â.

    Pathak warned that while recent outbreaks may wake people up, public urgency fades just as rapidly as it enters the headlines, like it did during the smaller spike in 2019.

    Sustaining confidence after the immediate threat subsides requires moving away from reactive, crisis-only warnings toward consistent, year-round engagement led by trusted âlocal messengers like pediatricians, school nurses and community health workers,â Pathak said.

    It has been revealed that still, attitudes about childhood vaccinations remain less favorable than in earlier decades. In 2001, 94% of people remarked vaccinations were very or extremely important. And a large gap still remains between Republicans and Democrats.

    Sources indicate that just 50% of Republicans believe that vaccines are very crucial, compared to 91% of Democrats. The data also shows that Republicans are more likely to say theyâve heard only about the negative effects of vaccines and have not heard about the benefits.

    Pathak declined to look at the issue through a purely partisan lens, instead blaming a broader shift against institutional trust fueled in part by fragmented information ecosystems.

    âOver the past decade â and accelerating sharply during the Covid-19 pandemic â public health guidance became entangled in wider debates over mandates, while algorithmic social media feeds sorted Americans into very different information environments,â Pathak mentioned.

    To close the gap in vaccine confidence, Pathak states public health experts must âlisten to familiesâ specific questions without judgment, communicate openly about both protective benefits and rare side effects, and use modern data/technology tools to spot emerging confusion early.â.

    âTop-down directives and dense statistical tables rarely persuade worried parents,â he added.

    It has been revealed that in November 2025, Kennedy Jr. directed the CDC to revise its website to suggest a connection between vaccines and autism, a departure from previous guidance.     Industry observers note that âSocial media stories still travel much faster than epidemiological studies â especially when parents navigating an autism diagnosis are searching online for answers,â Pathak mentioned. âData alone is not enough unless clinicians and public health communicators share it with empathy, clarity and respect.â.

    Just in the U.S., the CDC estimates routine childhood vaccinations have prevented approximately 508 million cases of illness, 32 million hospitalizations and over 1.1 million deaths, generating $2.7 trillion in societal savings.

    Associate Clinical Professor Nicole Ferschke at Northern Arizona University mentioned vaccination is one of the best ways to prevent the further spread of measles.

    Ferschke echoed Pathakâs concerns that the short-term uptick will not be sustained without increased efforts to improve trust in healthcare nationwide, which includes increasing access to vaccines and transparent, evidence-based communication.

    #125203. The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2218 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio.
    • In a recent development, the station later mentioned it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl.
    • Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. Newly introduced York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “Filthy Words” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

    In a recent development, the station later mentioned it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.”.

    Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he remarked was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. A member of Morality in Media who frequently listened to the station to “see how far” they’d go, Douglas later acknowledged that he had laughed out loud at the bit but “did not appreciate WBIA’s ‘smart-alecky’ on-air provocations.”.

    The previous year, Carlin had been arrested after performing an earlier version of the same routine, but a judge threw out the charge. This time, the FCC found the broadcast “indecent,” and put its order in the station’s license file.

    That order ended up before the Supreme Court.

    Recent findings suggest that early in its order, the FCC acknowledged that Congress had forbade it from censoring broadcasts. But Congress had also prohibited the broadcast of “obscene, indecent, or profane” language, and the Commission thought Carlin’s broadcast fit the bill. In the FCC’s view, the ban on “indecent” language covered not just obscenity, but also patently offensive language when there was a reasonable risk of children listening. Late at night, when children were unlikely to be listening, the same material might be okay if it appeared in a work of serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

    Two commissioners thought even that was too permissive. Charlotte Reid believed “this language to be totally inappropriate for broadcast at anytime” and thought the commission’s standard did “not go far enough.” Commissioner James Quello took much the same view. “Garbage is garbage,” he wrote, whether children were listening or not.

    The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, however, set aside the order in a 2-1 vote, with one judge believing it violated the statutory ban on censorship and the other saying it violated the First Amendment. The FCC appealed to the Supreme Court.

    According to recent reports, at oral argument, which was held in April of 1978, several justices made their distaste for Carlin’s bit plain. When Pacifica’s lawyer stressed that the station had warned listeners beforehand and aired the monologue as part of an educational program about language, Chief Justice Warren Burger incredulously asked, “This is educational in your view?” And when counsel defended the material’s artistic value, Justice Thurgood Marshall responded, “Well, I’m not an expert, but if that’s artistic, deliver me.” Justice William Rehnquist, for his part, tested the limits of Pacifica’s position with a hypothetical involving a single four-letter word repeated for an hour. Would the FCC be powerless to prohibit that? Justice John Paul Stevens, however, seemed troubled by the potential reach of the FCC’s position, given that the prohibition on indecency could be enforced through criminal law.

    One striking exchange concerned the Justice Department’s position to argue separately, and more narrowly, than the FCC. The solicitor general’s office urged that the First Amendment prevented the government from barring particular words outright for a substantial part of the day without regard to context, even if the FCC could constitutionally regulate “indecency” to some extent. Rehnquist sharply asked why the Justice Department was arguing against the FCC, what interest it had in seeking a narrow construction of an act of Congress, and whether the solicitor general, as the government’s lawyer, could ever argue that an act of Congress was unconstitutional.

    Justice Lewis Powell also pressed the DOJ on the reasons behind its departure from the FCC, noting that the DOJ had supported the FCC in the court below. “That is true, and that is an embarrassment to us,” Deputy Solicitor General Louis Claiborne acknowledged, suggesting it was because the matter had been handled there by the Antitrust Division rather than the Criminal Division. Another explanation, which he did not mention, was that the administration had changed.

    The court ultimately ruled 5-4 that the FCC could constitutionally treat this broadcast as “indecent” under the governing statute, and that the government could constitutionally prohibit indecency even though it fell short of legal obscenity. Stevens wrote for Burger, Justice Harry Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist, having apparently struggled with the case and flip-flopped before settling against Pacifica. The Commission had treated the piece as a nuisance, and, as the court had observed in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., a nuisance could be as simple as “a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.” He concluded that “when the Commission finds that a pig has entered the parlor, the exercise of its regulatory power does not depend on proof that the pig is obscene.” Though the holding expanded the government’s power to regulate speech, Stevens emphasized broadcasting’s pervasive presence in the home and its accessibility to children, the fact the piece was broadcast during the daytime, and the narrowness of the holding. He did not address late night broadcasts or the “occasional expletive.”.

    It has been revealed that stevens had only three votes for some parts of his opinion. Powell, joined by Blackmun, wrote separately to object to Stevens’ suggestion that the level of protection that speech receives should depend on a judge’s perception of that speech’s value. For them, the combination of repeated, patently offensive language, an afternoon broadcast, and children’s ready access was enough to resolve the case. Powell also addressed the concern that the decision could end up “reduc[ing] the adult population . . . to [hearing] only what is fit for children”: adults could buy tapes or hear the same words at theaters.

    It has been revealed that justice Potter Stewart dissented, joined by Justices William Brennan, Byron White, and Marshall. Stewart would have resolved the case on statutory grounds. He read “indecent” to reach only obscene material, and everyone agreed that Carlin’s monologue fell outside that category. His opinion recalled his concurrence in Jacobellis v. Ohio, where he voted to overturn an obscenity conviction for showing a French film with an explicit love scene. Stewart understood obscenity narrowly, but declined to define it, famously observing in that case, “I know it when I see it, and the motion picture involved in this case is not that.”.

    In a recent development, brennan wrote a separate dissent, joined by Marshall, that went further. He agreed with Stewart on the statute and noted he would ordinarily refrain from addressing the constitutional question, but he found “the Court’s misapplication of fundamental First Amendment principles so patent, and its attempt to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people so misguided,” that he was “unable to remain silent.”.

    In a recent development, brennan disputed the analogy between a radio broadcast and an intrusion into the home. Listeners voluntarily turn on the radio, and they can voluntarily turn it off. In perhaps his sharpest passage, he wrote:.

    Brennan also questioned the majority’s reliance on protecting children. He read the court’s precedents as allowing the government to shield children from material that was obscene as to them. In his view, Carlin’s routine fell outside that category. Keeping it off the radio during the afternoon cut off access for adults as well as children. And while the majority had invoked parents’ right to raise their children as they saw fit, Brennan thought the FCC had somewhat ironically made the choice for them.

    Sources indicate that finally, he remained unconvinced that the court’s reasoning would reach only cases like Carlin’s. Among the things it could sweep in were “literary works, novels, poems, and plays by the likes of Shakespeare, Joyce, Hemingway, Ben Jonson, Henry Fielding, Robert Burns, and Chaucer,” “a good deal of political speech, such as the Nixon tapes,” and even portions of the Bible. In his view, the public, and not the court, should have the power to weed out “worthless and offensive” speech in a marketplace “unsullied by the censor’s hand.”.

    According to recent reports, brennan and Marshall had joined together in another Supreme Court opinion involving the F-word. In Cohen v. California, they joined Justice John Harlan II’s opinion protecting the right to wear a jacket emblazoned with “Fuck the Draft.” Stewart joined it too (not surprisingly, Burger and Blackmun dissented). Brennan brought Cohen straight into his Pacifica dissent; as he made clear, changing the words can change what the speaker communicates, something that applies especially well to Carlin because the taboo words were themselves the subject of the routine. And Brennan thought telling listeners to buy a record or pay to see Carlin live missed what it meant to hear the routine on the radio.

    Sources indicate that in closing, Brennan wrote that the majority had only “confirm[ed] Carlin’s prescience as a social commentator.” (It was interesting that Marshall, who sounded distinctly unimpressed by the claim of artistic merit at oral argument, joined him, perhaps especially here.) As Brennan pointed out, Carlin had made fun of the rules about which words you could say on the air, and the court had exemplified the very attitude he was satirizing. To top it all off: Appended to the opinion is the transcript of Carlin’s routine, giving his “indecent” words a permanent home in the U.S. Reports.

    It has been revealed that at the 2002 Billboard Music Awards on Fox, Cher dispatched the critics who’d spent decades predicting her downfall with “So f*** ’em.” At the 2003 awards, Nicole Richie asked whether anyone had tried getting cow manure out of a Prada purse, then used the F-word to describe how hard it was. The next year, after Bono called U2’s Golden Globe win “really, really f***ing brilliant,” the FCC announced that even a single expletive could be indecent, and it later applied that approach to the two earlier Fox broadcasts.

    In 2009, the Supreme Court took up the dispute in FCC v. Fox Television Stations. Writing for a 5-4 majority, Justice Antonin Scalia held that the FCC had adequately explained its change in policy under the Administrative Procedure Act, leaving the First Amendment question open. Justice Clarence Thomas joined the majority but wrote separately to question Pacifica’s holding. On remand, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit struck down the policy as unconstitutionally vague.

    It has been revealed that the case returned to the Supreme Court in 2012 and all eight participating justices agreed on the result (Justice Sonia Sotomayor recused herself). Justice Anthony Kennedy’s opinion held that the FCC had failed to give Fox fair notice that fleeting expletives could trigger an indecency finding, but once again left both Pacifica and the First Amendment question open. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote separately to say that Pacifica was wrong from the start and deserved reconsideration. But while the court has had several cases involving curse words since, it has yet to take up the question directly.

    In 2004, the FCC dismissed complaints related to the airing of Saving Private Ryan on the basis that the film’s curse words helped convey the soldiers’ experience. But just two years later, it slapped a station with $15,000 in fines for airing a Martin Scorsese documentary about Blues music that contained profanity. In 2020, the FCC received over 1,300 complaints about Jennifer Lopez and Shakira’s halftime show, though it never took any action against the network. And in February 2026, FCC requested transcripts of Bad Bunny’s Superbowl halftime performance before ultimately finding no violation.

    Half a century after Carlin’s seven dirty words, the FCC’s continued and seemingly arbitrary application of its indecency laws shows the prescience of Brennan’s dissent and the need to finally answer the question of whether the Constitution prohibits the “dominant culture” from trying to force “groups who do not share its mores to conform to its way of acting, thinking, and speaking.”.

    Anastasia Boden is a Senior Attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, where she brings civil rights lawsuits that advance the Constitution’s promises of equality and economic opportunity.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A judge had issued a "gag order," barring the media from reporting on what was stated in open court by the daughters of farming tycoon Michael Abatti.

    (CN) â The Arizona Court of Appeals ruled Tuesday that news organizations can publish statements made, in open court, by the daughters of farming tycoon Michael Abatti, who is accused of shooting his estranged wife to death.

    “We are troubled that no one told the daughters the consequences of reading their statements in open court,” wrote Judge Jennifer Perkins in the unanimous opinion. “But once the daughters spoke in open court, the First Amendment protected the pressâs right to publish what they said, even if the failure to warn the daughters was inconsistent with the Victimsâ Bill of Rights.”.

    Abatti, a 63-year-old prominent farmer, is charged with first-degree murder in the death of his wife, 59-year-old Kerri Ann Abatti. The Imperial Valley couple had been embroiled in a bitter, three-year-long divorce, at the heart of which lay a $200 million trust. Arrested four weeks after the shooting, Abatti pleaded not guilty and is being held in custody, apparently unable to post the $5.5 million in bail.

    According to recent reports, at Abatti’s arraignment in December last year, his two daughters, who attended the hearing remotely, were allowed to read victim impact statements. A reporter from KPNX-TV Channel 12 was also listening to the proceedings remotely, with the court’s approval. The daughters’ statements were admitted into the record under seal, but they were also allowed to read them aloud during the hearing, which was open to the public. After the first statement was read, both the prosecutor and the defense attorney asked the court to issue a “gag order,” barring members of the media from reporting what the daughters said.

    According to recent reports, KPNX objected to the gag order, arguing it was unconstitutional prior restraint. But both Abatti and his daughters urged the judge to stand by the order, Abatti arguing that publishing the statements would taint the small-town jury pool, and the daughters arguing they didn’t know the hearing was a public forum. The judge kept the gag order in place, and KPNX, joined by a handful of other local media outlets, filed a petition to overrule the order.

    In a recent development, the three-judge panel found the gag order was unconstitutional under both the Arizona and U.S. Constitutions.

    “A court may not bar the press from publishing what happens in open court unless the ‘gravity of the evil’ resulting from publication, ‘discounted by its improbability, justifies such invasion of free speech as is necessary to avoid the danger,’” Perkins wrote, citing a 1976 Supreme Court ruling.

    As to the argument that the daughters’ statements would taint the jury pool, Perkins wrote, “Even if the small, rural community here increases the risk of jury prejudice, that risk remains too speculative … Abatti has not shown, for example, that ordinary tools â a larger jury pool, questioning prospective jurors about media exposure, and instructing jurors to consider only the trial evidence â would fail to protect him from prejudice caused by reporting on his daughtersâ statements.”.

    The panel found that while the daughters might be harmed by the publicizing of their comments, “the gravity of the potential emotional harm to the adult daughters does not justify the prior restraint.”.

    Judges Jon Saline and Samuel Clark rounded out the panel.

    Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, in September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion.
    • Recent findings suggest that since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view.
    • Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    According to recent reports, in September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”.

    Recent findings suggest that since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    According to recent reports, the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Denver posted a upcoming rule Friday stipulating attorneys and pro see parties certify human verification of all cited authorities and quotations, Law360 reports.

French data consultant Damien Charlotin found that court cases involving hallucinated case citations worldwide have decreased this year, which he attributes to hallucination awareness and LLM improvements.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • "When I started counting my blessings, my whole life turned around." â Willie Nelson.
    • Sources indicate that for many years, I spent much of November â from the 1st until Thanksgiving Day â posting to social media the things I was thankful for.
    • According to recent reports, not because Iâm not thankful.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    "When I started counting my blessings, my whole life turned around." â Willie Nelson.

    Sources indicate that for many years, I spent much of November â from the 1st until Thanksgiving Day â posting to social media the things I was thankful for. New day, new item of thanksgiving.

    According to recent reports, not because Iâm not thankful. I am. Perhaps more so than in a long time. And I have a lot to be thankful for, possibly more than ever in my life.

    I didnât this year because it had started to feel performative. Looking back through my Facebook memories, I saw Iâd just recycled the same concepts, often on the same dates, year after year.

    Iâm thankful for a warm home.

    Iâm thankful for my partner. For the kids.

    Iâm thankful we have more than enough to eat.

    Iâm thankful for music. For the arts.

    Recent findings suggest that iâm thankful when it rains. Or when it stops raining.

    Itâs true that Iâm still thankful for all those things. I hope I always will be. But this year I chose to keep the gratitude to myself. To see if something can still exist even if itâs not blasted across the socials.

    To be deliberately thankful, in my heart, rather than a broken record of low-hanging platitudes for the few whose algorithms are still aligned with mine to see and ignore.

    And to embrace a season of change for me that began around Thanksgiving last year and has leafed and branched like the giant oak tree across the street, huge and gnarled and somehow suddenly ancient but so, so alive.

    And something to tie our lives to now.

    I have written millions of words for Courthouse News over the last nearly 16 years. Complaint and ruling summaries, then news stories, then editing notes and endless emails and, too infrequently, a column.

    These are the last of them. The season of change that has become a giant oak tree sprouted an unforeseen branch that I find myself perched on now, my legs dangling high above the ground. Will it support my weight? My family? All our hopes and dreams?

    I donât know. The tree of change is still growing, still manifesting. The unknown looms large over the known. When it will stop and what it will finally be, I donât know.

    In a recent development, but we have each other. We have our health, we have our home. We have far more than we need.

    And books that will finally be read.

    Words written because I want to.

    Industry News: The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • On November 10, The New York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v.
    • According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    On November 10, The New York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller, in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”.

    According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

    The Times story has reverberated swiftly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used. Law professor Jonathan Adler, for example, has argued that the citation to Blackstone was one among many, and additional sources that Scalia cited used the “and” formulation. Others have responded that Scalia was anything but sloppy, which would be especially true when it came to such an influential and crucial source.

    It has been revealed that both sides, though, seem to be burying the lede. In my view, this is a story not about historical errors or the nuances of legal citation. Rather, it is about how judicial dicta that was never intended to lay down broad, permanent rules has taken on a life of its own, and how other justices on the Supreme Court subsequently canonized Scalia’s stray language by turning it into a “test” that would govern any number of future cases – when it’s not at all clear Scalia ever contemplated this or would have endorsed any such thing.

    Sources indicate that as most law students and lawyers are well aware, the holding-dicta distinction is deeply rooted in American jurisprudence: generally speaking, the holding is the analysis necessary to resolve the actual case before the court, and everything else in an opinion is dicta (this comes from the Latin phrase “obiter dictum,” or “remarked in passing”). Fundamental to that distinction is that dicta, while it may be persuasive, is not precedential. As Chief Justice John Marshall wrote in 1821, the reason for not deferring blindly to dicta is “obvious”:.

    The late Judge Richard Posner once similarly emphasized the risk that dicta “can be misleading if carelessly lifted from the case-specific contexts in which they were originally uttered … That is why courts in assessing the binding effect of previous decisions distinguish between the dicta, which are the inessential parts of the opinion, and the holding.” Circuits vary in their approach to Supreme Court dicta, generally deferring more heavily to such language when they find it thoroughly considered or supported, but the court is, of course, never bound by its own dicta.

    According to recent reports, in fact, Scalia himself was no fan of relying heavily on dicta from prior Supreme Court decisions. In a 1993 opinion, he criticized a group of dissenting justices by noting that their position found “support, if at all, only in the dicta of this Court’s opinions.” This was, in Scalia’s view, as good as no support at all. Indeed, Scalia rejected reliance on “drive-by … rulings” not fully considered by the issuing court, even if not purely dicta. In his 2015 decision for the court in Kerry v. Din, Scalia excoriated a proposition advanced in a dissenting opinion as resting solely on “dictum in a footnote” and then observed that “[t]he footnoted dictum that Justice Breyer proposes to elevate to constitutional law is a dangerous doctrine.” He further joined opinions that rejected prior dicta as unprincipled, especially when greater investigation revealed reasons for caution.

    According to recent reports, scalia’s position was nuanced – for example, he once joined a dissent by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg that endorsed reliance on certain dictum as persuasive – yet a cautious approach to dicta is consistent with his broader judicial philosophy as well. He was at times willing to jettison even precedential decisions squarely applicable to the case at hand when those decisions were contrary to original public meaning. Unconsidered dicta, presumably, would then be far lower in the pecking order.

    Returning to Heller and the phrase at issue, it’s hard to argue that the “dangerous and unusual” passage from Heller is anything but dicta. The issue in Heller was whether a Washington, D.C. ordinance “generally prohibit[ing] the possession of handguns” violated the Second Amendment, or if there was an individual right to keep arms for one’s self-defense. Scalia’s majority opinion answered in the affirmative, as “the American people have considered the handgun to be the quintessential self-defense weapon.” D.C. never argued that handguns were entirely exempt from protection because they were especially dangerous. The question of dangerous and/or unusual weapons was not at issue in the case; accordingly, it wasn’t thoroughly investigated through the adversarial process.

    Rather, after canvassing the historical evidence and concluding it supported an individual-rights view of the Second Amendment, Scalia turned to the nature of the right he had just explicated. In three short paragraphs not necessary to the holding, he explained why the amendment did not authorize gun keeping-and-carrying by anyone in any circumstance; rather history revealed limitations on the right, such as “the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’”.

    Whatever the purpose of this section – Justice John Paul Stevens later suggested the language was proposed by Justice Anthony Kennedy (the crucial fifth vote in Heller) in exchange for joining the majority – it was far from necessary to resolve the case at hand.

    Sources indicate that so how did such dicta become relevant? In the 2016 case Caetano v. Massachusetts, decided after Scalia had passed away, the justices unanimously overturned a Massachusetts Supreme Court decision upholding that state’s ban on stun guns in a criminal prosecution of a woman who used this weapon to defend herself from an abusive ex-boyfriend. Justice Samuel Alito issued a concurring opinion (joined by Justice Clarence Thomas) that performed an interesting maneuver. Seizing on the fact that the per curiam opinion in that case referenced Scalia’s “dangerous and unusual” formulation, Alito turned Scalia’s language into a doctrinal test: “As the per curiam opinion recognizes, this is a conjunctive test: A weapon may not be banned unless it is both dangerous and unusual.” But the per curiam had done no such thing; rather, that opinion simply cited the passage in Heller as referring to one limitation on the right to keep and bear arms. And the per curiam stated that the lower court in that case had faltered by concluding that any weapon not in common use in 1791 was per se unusual, not by failing to use a conjunctive test.

    (Ironically, Alito has his own well-publicized objections to giving past Supreme Court dicta undue veneration – his opinion for the court in Dobbs heavily suggested that Roe’s viability framework was entitled to less weight in the stare decisis analysis because it was initially mere dicta, “the Court’s own brainchild [for which n]either party advocated.”).

    According to recent reports, from there, the “dangerous and unusual” language took on a life of its own. In 2022’s Fresh York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, in which the court struck down New York’s concealed-carry law, the majority set forth a test for Second Amendment constitutionality privileging historical evidence above all else. At the first step of that test, a court determines whether the conduct at matter is protected by the right to keep and bear arms, which is where the exclusion of dangerous and/or unusual weapons becomes relevant. If the banned weapon is not protected by the Second Amendment (for, say, being “dangerous and unusual”), a constitutional challenge is dead on arrival. If, on the other hand, the plaintiff can show the weapons are protected, then the burden switches to the government to provide historical evidence to support its regulation. (The consequences may be even greater, as some have argued that “usualness” (or “common use”) conclusively establishes not only threshold protection for the weapon but also that any legislative ban is ahistorical and thus unconstitutional.).

    This test has divided the judiciary in recent years. For example, a Massachusetts federal judge evaluating a challenge to that state’s AR-15 ban recognized the apparent disconnect between Heller and Blackstone but nevertheless noted that “the Supreme Court has expressly stated . . .that the relevant tradition is one of regulating ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’” The Massachusetts judge found these weapons were not in “common use,” and, in any event, a historical tradition of responding to technological advances by regulating specific weapons supported the ban. By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit interpreted Scalia’s language to signal that widespread ownership of AR-15s and large-capacity magazines meant any legislative attempt to ban them was unconstitutional. The “dangerous and unusual” framework has led other judges on a search for ownership statistics and sales data to assess a weapon’s popularity, triggering sharp debate over whether a test that ultimately turns on commonality is even workable.

    It has been revealed that this is particularly relevant since the court is presently preparing to hear oral argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, a Second Amendment challenge to state and local bans on AR-15s, on December 2. While the recent attention to Scalia’s citation may trigger discussion at oral argument, most justices are now likely to treat “dangerous and unusual” as an established standard and ownership statistics as definitive proof that AR-15s are not unusual and thus protected. Absent from this, however, will be the fact that this standard did not emerge from any well-reasoned, litigation-tested analysis making it deserve deference in the first place – especially under Scalia’s own approach to judging.

    The debate over Scalia’s Blackstone citation, then, has obscured a more important problem: the Supreme Court’s decision to treat its past dicta as doctrine that can settle the outcome of cases on which the court has never passed.

    Andrew Willinger is an Assistant Professor at Georgia State University College of Law, where he teaches constitutional law and civil procedure.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The U.S. Department of Justice Museum opened earlier this year as part of the festivities surrounding the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. In a blog post shared on Monday, the Justice Department celebrated a Supreme Court-related addition to the museum’s collection: “a morning suit worn by Solicitor General Noel J. Francisco during his arguments on behalf of the United States government before the Supreme Court.”.

    In a recent development, on Monday, the Supreme Court dismissed lead plaintiff Cutberto Viramontes from Viramontes v. Cook County, a case on the constitutionality of bans on AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles that is scheduled to be argued on Wednesday, December 2. The case is expected to proceed without Viramontes’ involvement, although the case name will now be Khaya v. Cook County. For more on this move, see the Morning Reads section below.

    The Supreme Court Building will be closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday and Friday.

    The December argument session will begin on Monday, November 30. As noted above, on Wednesday, December 2, at 10 a.m. EST, the court will hear argument in a major Second Amendment case. We will be live blogging that morning beginning at 9:30 a.m.

    BigLaw firms, hunting for senior-level talent as they try to expand client relationships, are increasingly hiring lawyers with in-house legal department experience.

    Over the past five years, Am Law 200 law firms hired about 740 lawyers from in-house positions. These in-house lawyers began their careers in firms, according to a story by Law.com.

    Lawyers who have switched from firms to in-house and then back to firms are being calling “boomerangs” in the legal industry, according to a FirmProspects report this month.

    Firms’ increasing investment in artificial intelligence also has them searching for lateral partners who have an expertise in AI or are open to increasing their understanding and use of it, according to Law.com.

    Industry News: What do these Supreme Court plaintiffs have in common?
